implementation_notes: The async-Rust bulkhead is tokio::sync::Semaphore: a const-constructible permit counter per dependency, acquire().await for the bounded wait (tokio's timeout combinators bound it), try_acquire() for the fail-fast path, and a Permit whose Drop releases the slot, so ownership replaces manual release bookkeeping. Use it when the dependency call is asynchronous; for blocking clients prefer the dedicated-runtime variant, and when the call is part of a tower service stack the ConcurrencyLimit layer expresses the same bound as a composable layer.

variants.name: tokio::sync::Semaphore permits
variants.implementation_notes: The async-Rust bulkhead is tokio::sync::Semaphore: a const-constructible permit counter per dependency, acquire().await for the bounded wait (tokio's timeout combinators bound it), try_acquire() for the fail-fast path, and a Permit whose Drop releases the slot, so ownership replaces manual release bookkeeping. Use it when the dependency call is asynchronous; for blocking clients prefer the dedicated-runtime variant, and when the call is part of a tower service stack the ConcurrencyLimit layer expresses the same bound as a composable layer.
pitfalls: try_acquire also returns Err when the semaphore is closed, so rejection and shutdown must be distinguished in error mapping.
tokio's Semaphore is fair and waiting acquires queue; under overload that queue is unbounded unless you use try_acquire or a timeout.
Holding a permit across unrelated awaits serialises the dependency needlessly; keep the guarded region to the dependency call.
Blocking clients called inside an async task while holding a permit stall a runtime worker; offload with spawn_blocking or a dedicated runtime.

variants.name: tower ConcurrencyLimit layer (service stack)
variants.implementation_notes: When dependencies are tower services (hyper clients, gRPC, database proxies) the bulkhead is a layer: ConcurrencyLimitLayer::new(n) wraps a client so at most n in-flight requests pass downstream while callers wait on readiness; combine it with a load-shedding layer for the fail-fast rejection policy and with a timeout for the deadline. This composes with retry and rate-limit layers and keeps the bound next to the client construction; use the semaphore variant when the call is not a Service or admission must be shared across clients.
pitfalls: The layer bounds in-flight requests but readiness-based callers queue; without load shedding, saturation becomes latency instead of rejection.
Layer order matters: concurrency inside versus outside the timeout changes whether queued time counts against the deadline.
Cloning the wrapped service shares the limit internally; verify that sharing matches the intended per-dependency boundary.
ConcurrencyLimit requires tower's Service contract, so adapting plain async functions adds boilerplate compared with a semaphore.

variants.name: dedicated tokio runtime for blocking dependencies
variants.implementation_notes: Hard thread isolation: build a separate multi-thread runtime with a fixed worker_threads count for a blocking dependency (or a group of them) and submit its work there, so a stuck blocking client consumes only that runtime's threads and never the API runtime's workers; spawn_blocking on the main runtime (bounded by max_blocking_threads) is the lighter alternative when a dedicated runtime per dependency is too heavy. Prefer it when the dependency has no async client or when a library blocks unpredictably.
pitfalls: Threads and stacks are reserved per runtime even when idle; many per-dependency runtimes multiply memory.
A runtime must not be dropped from inside itself; keep it in a struct or static and shut it down explicitly.
Results are not Send across runtimes without a channel bridge such as oneshot or mpsc.
max_blocking_threads is global (default 512), so an unconfigured blocking workload can still exhaust the main runtime's blocking pool.
try_acquire also returns Err when the semaphore is closed, so rejection and shutdown must be distinguished in error mapping.
tokio's Semaphore is fair and waiting acquires queue; under overload that queue is unbounded unless you use try_acquire or a timeout.
Holding a permit across unrelated awaits serialises the dependency needlessly; keep the guarded region to the dependency call.
Blocking clients called inside an async task while holding a permit stall a runtime worker; offload with spawn_blocking or a dedicated runtime.
